parent: The First Dhyāna: Marks of Realization

zh: 第二、明支義，亦開為三：一、釋支名；二、釋支義；三、辨支相。第一、釋支名者，初禪有五支：一、覺支；二、觀支；三、喜支；四、樂支；五、一心支。覺者初心覺悟，名為覺。觀者，後細心分別，名為觀。慶悅之心，名為喜。恬澹之心，名為樂。寂然不散，名一心。所以制五支者，若對不善，即為破五欲、五蓋；若對善法，即對行五法。故《釋論》云：「離五蓋，行五法，具五支，入初禪。」
en: Second, clarifying the meaning of the factors: this, too, opens into three parts — explaining the name "factor"; explaining the meaning of "factor"; and distinguishing the marks of the factors.

First, explaining the name "factor": the first dhyāna has five factors — the factor of initial thought; the factor of sustained reflection; the factor of joy; the factor of happiness; and the factor of one-pointedness of mind. Initial thought is the initial mind's own awakening, and is called "initial thought." Sustained reflection is the subsequent fine mind's own discrimination, and is called "sustained reflection." A mind of celebration and delight is called "joy." A mind of tranquil ease is called "happiness." Being still and undispersed is called "one-pointedness of mind." As for why these five factors are established: with reference to the unwholesome, they serve to break through the five desires and the five hindrances; with reference to the wholesome dharmas, they correspond to the practice of the five dharmas. Hence the Exegetical Treatise says: "Leaving behind the five hindrances, practicing the five dharmas, complete in the five factors — one enters the first dhyāna."

zh: 第二、釋支義者，如《纓絡經》說：「禪名支林。」此即據總別之明義也。言支者，支離為義。如因樹根莖，則有枝條。根莖是一，枝條有異。禪中支義亦爾，從一定心出生五支，此是總中別義。所言林者，如林因眾多樹，得有林名。禪義亦爾，五支和合，總受禪稱。此即據別中之總，故知若說禪，即知有五支，如聞林名，必知有樹及以枝條。復次，有人言：「枝持為義。」如欲界、未到地中雖有單靜定心，未有覺觀等五支共相枝持，則定心淺薄易失。若得初禪，即有覺觀等法，則定心安隱，牢固難壞。
en: Second, explaining the meaning of "factor": as the Yingluo Sūtra says, "dhyāna is named a grove of factors" — this is precisely a statement made with reference to both the general and the particular senses of the term together. As for "factor": its meaning is that of branching apart. It is like a tree: because of its root and trunk, it has branches and twigs; the root and trunk are one, while the branches and twigs are many and varied. The meaning of "factor" within dhyāna is exactly the same — from a single concentrated mind, five factors come forth; this is the particular sense within the general. As for "grove": it is like a grove, which, because of its many trees together, comes to be called a grove. The meaning of "dhyāna" is exactly the same: the five factors combined together, taken as a whole, receive the name "dhyāna." This is precisely the general sense within the particular. Hence it is known that, whenever "dhyāna" is spoken of, the five factors are thereby already implied, just as, upon hearing the name "grove," one already knows there must be trees, and branches and twigs as well.

Furthermore, some say: "the meaning is that of branching support." Just as, within desire-realm concentration and the "not-yet-arrived" state, although a single, still, concentrated mind is present, the five factors — initial thought, sustained reflection, and the rest — are not yet present together to sustain it like branches, and so the concentrated mind remains shallow and slight, easily lost; but once the first dhyāna is attained, the dharmas of initial thought, sustained reflection, and the rest are all present, and the concentrated mind is thereby made secure and firm, difficult to break apart.

zh: 三、辨支相。若數人辨相，正約二十二心數去取辨五支相，具出彼義（云云）。今家所明，略為二：一者、別；二者、通。一、別釋五支相者。云何名覺？覺名觸覺，有二種：一、成禪覺；二、壞禪覺。如有風，能成雨，有風能壞雨，如上所說。十六觸中，一觸有十種善法眷屬安隱莊嚴者，是成禪覺，如上說。一觸有二十惡法，是壞禪覺。復次，覺者，覺屬身根，為身有情，異乎木石，所以對觸故生覺。如經說見聞覺知義。見屬於眼，聞屬於耳，鼻、觸覺屬於身，知屬於意，亦對舌也，有增用故。
en: Third, distinguishing the marks of the factors: if the Abhidharma masters distinguish these marks, they do so strictly with reference to the twenty-two mental factors, taking up and setting aside among them to distinguish the marks of the five factors — their own sense is set out there in full (and so on). What this school clarifies is, in brief, of two kinds: the particular; and the general.

First, explaining the marks of the five factors particularly. What is meant by "initial thought"? Initial thought means tactile awareness, and is of two kinds: initial thought that accomplishes dhyāna; and initial thought that ruins dhyāna. It is like wind: there is a wind able to bring rain, and a wind able to ruin rain, exactly as already described above. Within the sixteen tactile sensations, whichever sensation carries the ten kinds of wholesome dharma as its retinue, peacefully adorning it, is initial thought that accomplishes dhyāna, as already described above; whichever sensation carries the twenty unwholesome dharmas instead is initial thought that ruins dhyāna. Furthermore, initial thought, as awareness, belongs to the body-faculty, since a body possessed of sentience differs from wood or stone, and so, in response to a tactile sensation, an awareness arises. As the sūtra speaks of the meaning of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: seeing belongs to the eye; hearing belongs to the ear; smell and tactile sensing belong to the body; and knowing belongs to the mind — though it also applies to the tongue, since it has an additional function there as well.

zh: 問曰：如經中說六觸因緣生受，何得覺觸但屬於身耶？答曰：此對通說。若通時，見中亦說聞，餘義類爾。今就別義論覺支者，正對身也。於未到定中發十六觸，觸於身根生識，覺前觸相，故名覺支。復次，覺名驚悟。行者得初禪，未曾所得善法諸功德故，心大驚悟。昔常為欲火所燒，得初禪時，如人入清涼池。但此覺生時，與欲界身根生覺有異。何以故？與定等善法一時俱發。是以偈言：「如貧得寶藏，大喜覺動心。」故言初心麁念名為覺。此與數人明義，應有小異。料簡（云云）。
en: Question: as the sūtra says that the six kinds of contact, through causes and conditions, give rise to sensation — how, then, can "sensing contact" belong only to the body? Answer: this is spoken of in general terms. When spoken of generally, "seeing" is also said to include "hearing," and the same holds for the rest by the same pattern; here, however, discussing "initial thought" in its particular sense, it corresponds precisely to the body. Within the "not-yet-arrived" concentration, the sixteen tactile sensations arise, coming into contact with the body-faculty and giving rise to consciousness, aware of the mark of the sensation that has just occurred — hence this is named the factor of initial thought.

Furthermore, "initial thought" also means being startled into awakening: the practitioner, attaining the first dhyāna, having never before attained such wholesome dharma and merit, the mind is greatly startled into awakening. Having long been burned by the fire of desire, upon attaining the first dhyāna, it is like a person entering a cool, refreshing pool. Yet this awakening, when it arises, differs from the awakening that arises through the body-faculty within the desire realm — why is this? Because it arises together, at one and the same time, with concentration and the other wholesome dharmas. Hence the verse says: "Like a poor person finding a buried treasure: great joy, and initial thought stirring the mind." Hence it is said that the initial mind's coarse thought is what is called "initial thought." This should differ slightly from how the Abhidharma masters clarify the same sense — this is to be examined further (and so on).

zh: 二、釋觀支者，後細心分別，名為觀。既分別觸發已，正念之心思量分別，向觸生時，與欲界中善法及未到等法大有異。所以者何？於此觸中有種種善法珍寶，與觸俱發，欲界所無。復次，分別者，分別十六觸中法寶之相亦不同，知麁則離，知善則修，此細心分別，故名觀支，故經說：「分別則為觀。」問曰：若爾，覺有何等異？答曰：如論說：「麁心在緣，名為覺；細心分別，名為觀。」又問：如《毘曇》中說：「覺觀在一心中。」今云何為二？答曰：二法雖在一心，二相不俱，謂覺時觀不明了，觀時覺不明了。譬如撞鐘，鐘聲雖一，而麁細有異。一心中覺觀亦如是。復次，身根、身識相應，名為覺；意根、意識相應，名為觀。身識是外鈍，故名麁；意識是內利，故能分別名細。此雖同緣一觸，而二相不俱，故為觀支。
en: Second, explaining the factor of sustained reflection: the subsequent fine mind's own discrimination is called "sustained reflection." Having already discriminated the sensation's own arising, the mind of right mindfulness deliberates and discriminates further, recognizing that, the moment the sensation first arose, it was already vastly different from any wholesome dharma of the desire realm or the "not-yet-arrived" state. Why is this? Because, within this very sensation, various treasures of wholesome dharma are present, arising together with it — treasures the desire realm itself does not possess at all. Furthermore, "discrimination" here means distinguishing that the marks of the dharma-treasures within the sixteen tactile sensations are themselves not all the same — recognizing the coarse, one leaves it behind; recognizing the wholesome, one cultivates it further — and this fine mind's own discrimination is what is named the factor of sustained reflection. Hence the sūtra says: "Discrimination is what is called sustained reflection."

Question: if this is so, how does this differ from initial thought? Answer: as the treatise says: "A coarse mind resting on its object is called initial thought; a fine mind discriminating is called sustained reflection." A further question: the Abhidharma says that initial thought and sustained reflection occur within a single mind — how, then, can they now be said to be two? Answer: although the two dharmas occur within a single mind, their two marks are not present simultaneously — that is, when initial thought is present, sustained reflection is not yet clear, and when sustained reflection is present, initial thought is no longer clear. It is like striking a bell: although the bell's sound is a single sound, it nonetheless has a coarse phase and a fine phase, differing from one another. Initial thought and sustained reflection within a single mind are exactly the same. Furthermore: correspondence with the body-faculty and body-consciousness is called initial thought; correspondence with the mind-faculty and mind-consciousness is called sustained reflection. Body-consciousness is outwardly dull, and so is called coarse; mind-consciousness is inwardly sharp, and so is able to discriminate, and is called fine. Although these two take the very same single sensation as their common object, their two marks are not present together — hence this is the factor of sustained reflection.

zh: 三、明喜支者，見細心分別思量，覺知十六觸等微妙珍寶，昔所未逢，是以心喜慶悅。又知所失欲樂甚少，今得初禪功德，其樂甚多。如是覺觀，利我不少，深心慶悅，踊躍無量，故名喜支。四、樂支者，行者於歡喜已後，其心恬然，受於觸中之樂，樂法娛心，安隱恬愉，故名樂支。問曰：喜樂有何異？答曰：如上覺觀分別，今喜樂亦爾。麁樂名喜，細樂名樂，亦可言麁喜為喜，細喜為樂。復次，喜樂雖俱是歡悅之相，而二相有異。喜根相應，故名喜；樂根相應，故名樂。踊躍心中，故名喜；恬靜心中，故名樂。復次，行者初緣得樂，心生歡喜，未及受樂，名喜；後緣喜情既息，以樂自娛，故名樂。譬如饑人得食，初得歡喜，未及受其味，故名喜；後得食之，方受味中之樂，故名樂。又如三禪有樂而無喜，故知二根有異。五、一心支者，經久受樂心息，雖有覺觸等事，而心不緣。既無分散，定住寂靜，故名一心支。此則略說初禪五支，次第而發，並據成就，立於支義。
en: Third, clarifying the factor of joy: seeing, through the fine mind's own discrimination and deliberation, that one has come to be aware of the subtle treasures within the sixteen tactile sensations, never before encountered — the mind is thereby joyful and delighted. Knowing, further, that what was lost, the pleasure of desire, was exceedingly slight, while what is now gained, the merit of the first dhyāna, is a pleasure exceedingly great: such initial thought and sustained reflection benefit oneself no small amount, and a deeply celebratory mind, leaping with joy beyond measure, is what is named the factor of joy.

Fourth, the factor of happiness: the practitioner, after this joy, the mind grown tranquil, receives the happiness present within the sensation itself — the dharma of happiness delighting the mind, at peace and content — this is named the factor of happiness. Question: how do joy and happiness differ? Answer: exactly as initial thought and sustained reflection were distinguished above, joy and happiness follow the same pattern: coarse pleasure is named joy, and fine pleasure is named happiness; or, alternatively, it may be said that coarse joy is joy, and fine joy is happiness. Furthermore, although joy and happiness are both marks of delight, the two marks nonetheless differ: correspondence with the joy-faculty is named joy; correspondence with the happiness-faculty is named happiness. A mind leaping with excitement is named joy; a mind at tranquil rest is named happiness. Furthermore: when the practitioner first takes happiness as an object, the mind gives rise to joy but has not yet actually received the happiness itself — this is named joy; afterward, once the sense of joy has come to rest, delighting in the happiness itself — this is named happiness. It is like a hungry person obtaining food: at first obtaining it, joy arises, but its taste has not yet actually been received — this is named joy; afterward, actually eating it, one then receives the happiness within its taste — this is named happiness. And, further still, the third dhyāna has happiness but no joy at all — hence it is known that these two faculties genuinely differ from one another.

Fifth, the factor of one-pointedness of mind: after happiness has long been received, the mind of happiness comes to rest; although the events of initial thought and sensation are still present, the mind no longer takes them as its object. Being now free of any scattering, concentration abides in stillness — this is named the factor of one-pointedness of mind. This, in brief, describes the first dhyāna's five factors, arising in sequence, and, with reference to their completion, establishes the meaning of "factor."

zh: 問曰：若爾，約十六觸，一觸皆有五義不？答曰：實爾，故知初禪對緣即有眾多支也。雖復對觸有多，終不出五支。譬如五陰，若對五根，根根說五，雖復眾多，而不可說言有第六陰。五支亦爾。二者、約通義明五支即一。覺發時，具有五支義。云何當覺發時，本對於觸，覺觸中冷暖即是覺支，當覺時豈不即分別？知冷異暖，即是觀支。當觸發時，即有喜心，如人見好美色，即生喜悅，不待思量，故論偈說：「大喜覺動心。」觸發之時，必舉體怡解，即是樂支。解發必與定俱，故名覺觀俱三昧，當知即有一心支。此則五支一時而發，不待成就，但於事未顯，故據成而說。別義如前。問曰：若爾，心便並慮？答曰：心雖不俱，法並何過？此類如十大地、心王、心數之義。問曰：若通支有五者，五支應有二十五？答曰：如佛經中說五陰，一陰有五，五五二十有五，而不乖五陰之義。通五支義亦如是。
en: Question: if this is so, then with reference to the sixteen tactile sensations, does each single sensation carry all five factors? Answer: it does indeed — hence it is known that the first dhyāna, in meeting its objects, has a great many factors. Yet, however many there may be in meeting the sensations, they never go beyond the five factors. It is like the five aggregates: with reference to the five sense-faculties, five aggregates are spoken of for each faculty in turn, and, although they are thereby many, one cannot say that there is a sixth aggregate. The five factors are exactly the same.

Second, clarifying, in the general sense, that the five factors are one. When initial thought arises, it already carries the sense of all five factors. How so? When initial thought arises, it is basically in response to a tactile sensation: being aware of the cold or warmth within the sensation is precisely the factor of initial thought; and, at the very moment of this awareness, how could there not already be discrimination? Knowing cold to differ from warmth is precisely the factor of sustained reflection. When the sensation arises, a mind of joy is already present — just as a person seeing a lovely form is delighted at once, without waiting to deliberate; hence the treatise verse says, "great joy, and initial thought stirring the mind." When the sensation arises, the whole body is necessarily suffused with ease and release — this is precisely the factor of happiness. This release necessarily arises together with concentration, and hence it is named the samādhi joined with initial thought and sustained reflection; one should know that the factor of one-pointedness of mind is already present as well. Thus the five factors arise at one and the same time, without waiting for their completion; it is simply that this is not yet evident in experience, and so the account above was given with reference to their completion. The particular sense is as already given above.

Question: if this is so, does the mind then deliberate on several things at once? Answer: although the mind itself is not plural, what fault is there in its dharmas occurring together? This is comparable to the sense of the ten universal mental factors, the mind-king, and its mental factors. Question: if each general factor contains five, should the five factors not then come to twenty-five? Answer: just as the Buddha's sūtras speak of the five aggregates — each aggregate containing five, five times five making twenty-five — without departing from the meaning of "five aggregates," so too is the general sense of the five factors.

The root-and-branch / grove-and-trees double image for 支 (factor) captures something genuinely subtle: dhyāna is one concentrated mind branching out into many parts (particular-in-general, like a single root and trunk sending out its branches) and simultaneously many parts gathered under one name (general-in-particular, like "grove" implying its trees) — neither reduction fully applies. The bell simile for initial thought and sustained reflection solves a real problem the Abhidharma tradition itself debates: how can two supposedly simultaneous mental factors both occur "within a single mind" without being literally concurrent? By making them phases of one continuous event (a bell's sound is one sound with a coarse onset and fine decay) rather than two competing events, the treatise dissolves the puzzle rather than resolving it by fiat. The hungry-person simile for joy versus happiness is worth remembering going forward: joy is the anticipatory delight of first securing something good, happiness is the settled savoring that follows — and the text flags in advance that the third dhyāna will have the second without the first, evidence that these really are separate faculties and not just intensity-grades of the same thing.

quiz.q: What are the five factors of the first dhyāna?
options: initial thought, sustained reflection, joy, happiness, one-pointedness
quiz.why: "The first dhyāna has five factors — the factor of initial thought; the factor of sustained reflection; the factor of joy; the factor of happiness; and the factor of one-pointedness of mind."

quiz.q: Why are five factors established, and what does the Exegetical Treatise say?
options: against the unwholesome they break the five desires and hindrances; with the wholesome they correspond to the five practiced dharmas; "leaving the hindrances, practicing the five dharmas, complete in the five factors, one enters the first dhyāna"
quiz.why: "As for why these five factors are established: with reference to the unwholesome, they serve to break through the five desires and the five hindrances; with reference to the wholesome dharmas, they correspond to the practice of the five dharmas. Hence the Exegetical Treatise says: 'Leaving behind the five hindrances, practicing the five dharmas, complete in the five factors — one enters the first dhyāna.'"

quiz.q: How does the text explain the "factor" and "grove" in "grove of factors"?
options: "factor" means branching, like branches from one trunk — five from one mind (the particular within the general); "grove" is many trees forming a grove — five together named dhyāna (the general within the particular)
quiz.why: "As for 'factor': its meaning is that of branching apart. It is like a tree ... from a single concentrated mind, five factors come forth; this is the particular sense within the general. As for 'grove': it is like a grove, which, because of its many trees together, comes to be called a grove ... the five factors combined together, taken as a whole, receive the name 'dhyāna.'"

quiz.q: Initial thought may accomplish or ruin dhyāna. What simile is used, and how are they told apart?
options: like wind that brings or ruins rain; a sensation with the ten wholesome retinue accomplishes dhyāna, one with the twenty unwholesome ruins it
quiz.why: "Initial thought means tactile awareness, and is of two kinds: initial thought that accomplishes dhyāna; and initial thought that ruins dhyāna. It is like wind: there is a wind able to bring rain, and a wind able to ruin rain ... whichever sensation carries the twenty unwholesome dharmas instead is initial thought that ruins dhyāna."

quiz.q: To which faculty does the text say initial thought belongs?
options: the body-faculty: the sensation contacts the body and gives rise to consciousness
quiz.why: "Discussing 'initial thought' in its particular sense, it corresponds precisely to the body. Within the 'not-yet-arrived' concentration, the sixteen tactile sensations arise, coming into contact with the body-faculty and giving rise to consciousness ... hence this is named the factor of initial thought." Sustained reflection corresponds to the mind-faculty.

quiz.q: The Abhidharma says initial thought and sustained reflection are in one mind. Why does the text still treat them as two, and what simile is used?
options: though in one mind, their marks are not simultaneous; like striking a bell, one sound with a coarse and a fine phase
quiz.why: "Although the two dharmas occur within a single mind, their two marks are not present simultaneously — that is, when initial thought is present, sustained reflection is not yet clear, and when sustained reflection is present, initial thought is no longer clear. It is like striking a bell: although the bell's sound is a single sound, it nonetheless has a coarse phase and a fine phase."

quiz.q: According to the treatise cited, how do initial thought and sustained reflection differ?
options: a coarse mind resting on its object is initial thought; a fine mind discriminating is sustained reflection
quiz.why: "As the treatise says: 'A coarse mind resting on its object is called initial thought; a fine mind discriminating is called sustained reflection.'" Body-consciousness is outwardly dull (coarse) and mind-consciousness inwardly sharp (fine).

quiz.q: For the other sense of initial thought, "being startled awake," which verse line is cited?
options: like a poor person finding treasure, great joy stirs the mind
the two dharmas disturb the mind
quiz.why: "Furthermore, 'initial thought' also means being startled into awakening: the practitioner, attaining the first dhyāna, having never before attained such wholesome dharma and merit, the mind is greatly startled into awakening ... Hence the verse says: 'Like a poor person finding a buried treasure, great joy stirs and moves the mind.'"

quiz.q: What simile shows the difference between joy and happiness?
options: a hungry person obtaining food: joy on getting it before tasting, happiness on eating and tasting it
quiz.why: "It is like a hungry person obtaining food: at first obtaining it, joy arises, but its taste has not yet actually been received — this is named joy; afterward, actually eating it, one then receives the happiness within its taste — this is named happiness."

quiz.q: The text says the third dhyāna has happiness but no joy. What does this prove?
options: the joy-faculty and the happiness-faculty genuinely differ
quiz.why: "Correspondence with the joy-faculty is named joy; correspondence with the happiness-faculty is named happiness ... And, further still, the third dhyāna has happiness but no joy at all — hence it is known that these two faculties genuinely differ from one another."

quiz.q: How does the factor of one-pointedness arise?
options: after long receiving happiness the mind rests; though sensations remain, it no longer takes them as object, abiding still
quiz.why: "After happiness has long been received, the mind of happiness comes to rest; although the events of initial thought and sensation are still present, the mind no longer takes them as its object. Being now free of any scattering, concentration abides in stillness — this is named the factor of one-pointedness of mind."
